description:
On develop 13d4783d0 this prints :three on interp and 3 on run and build. Elixir prints :three.

  def pick(3), do: :three
  def pick(n), do: n
  def call([fun | _], entry), do: fun.(entry)
  def main(), do: dbg(call([&pick/1], 3))

The same miss shows through Stream.map (its mappers sit in a list): Enum.to_list(Stream.map([1, 2, 3], &pick/1)) gives [1, 2, 3], and a clause that raises is skipped silently. A function passed as a plain parameter or inside a tuple is right, and so is a guard (when n == 3).

Mechanism (proven by a unit test that fails before the fix): a function called out of a list is compiled once for a type variable (pick/1[a0]). Native codegen folds a matching equality to false when Types::is_value_disjoint says the two operand types share no value (lower_eq_binop). Descr::erase_nominal left a type variable as it was, so `a0` and `int` intersected in nothing and the literal test became a constant miss. The interpreter does not fold, so it was right. The backend dump is identical on interp and run.

Fix: a type variable erases to any in the value-disjointness question, as an opaque does. It stands for whatever value arrives in its place.

Acceptance: the unit test; the program above with the case, atom, Stream and raising variants as an oracle fixture on interp, run and build; the full suite passes.

Found while writing the fixture for fz-sc8.102. Probes: /Users/j5n/Workspace/fz-sc8.102-probes/lp_*.fz and sm_*.fz.
title: A literal pattern matches in code compiled for a type variable
